analysis.one_liner: Transfers a national forest site sacred to Apache tribes to a copper mining company for mining.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee for nearly two years, with one subcommittee hearing, and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require the federal government to trade about 2,422 acres of Tonto National Forest land in Arizona — known as Oak Flat — to Resolution Copper Mining, LLC for use as a large copper mine. In exchange, the company would hand over roughly 5,300 acres of its own land in Arizona for conservation, protect the surface of Apache Leap, and pay the government an adjustment if copper production exceeded a baseline set in the bill's appraisal. The bill also would convey small parcels to the town of Superior. The federal land involved sits on one of the largest undeveloped copper deposits in North America, and the exchange had been debated for years before this version.
analysis.who_benefits: Resolution Copper Mining, LLC, which would receive full title to the federal land containing the copper deposit — a permanent private asset instead of conditional mining claims. The town of Superior and nearby communities would also gain land conveyances and, according to the bill's own findings, mining jobs in an area with high unemployment [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill 'authorizes and directs' the Secretary of Agriculture to convey the federal land in Pinal County to Resolution Copper, making it available for mining under the laws governing private land [S2][S3].

In exchange, the United States would receive roughly 5,300 acres of Resolution Copper land, including parcels added to the San Pedro Riparian and Las Cienegas National Conservation Areas and to the national forest system [S3].

Resolution Copper would have to surrender, without compensation, its rights to mine commercially under Apache Leap, and the government could issue only limited permits for underground work that would not disturb the surface [S2][S3].

The bill requires annual production reports and a value adjustment payment to the United States if copper production from the conveyed land exceeds the quantity assumed in the appraisal's income analysis; the money is earmarked for Forest Service and BLM maintenance [S3].
The bill directs the Secretary to convey land to the town of Superior, Arizona, for the fairview cemetery and airport-area parcels, with the town paying market value [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If the bill passed, the public would permanently lose Oak Flat — a campsite and recreation area in the Tonto National Forest that is sacred to Apache tribes — and the United States would give up land containing a very large copper deposit. Once the land is private, copper mined from it would be governed by private-land rules rather than the federal mining-claim system, which historically collected no royalty on production; the bill's own payment mechanism only applies above an appraisal-defined baseline [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Tribal nations, recreation users, federal landholders

drawbacks.text: The conveyance would be mandatory, not discretionary: the Secretary is 'authorized and directed' to hand over the land once Resolution Copper offers its parcels, removing the agency's normal ability to weigh a swap [S3].

The environmental review of the mine would happen only after the land is conveyed and a mine plan is submitted, with a three-year deadline for completion, and the review would be the basis for all federal decisions on the mine and its power, water, tailings, and waste facilities [S3].

The appraisal of the federal land would not need to be reappraised for three years — and not at all once an exchange agreement is signed — and improvements Resolution Copper made before the deal would be excluded from the federal land's appraised value [S3].

Because the conveyed land would be private, mining would proceed under private-land rules, and the bill states that nothing in it may interfere with Resolution Copper's existing unpatented mining claims on the federal parcel [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles real conservation gains — several thousand acres added to national conservation areas and forests, plus Apache Leap surface protection and a production payment — with a permanent transfer of federal land that is sacred to Apache tribes and sits over a major copper deposit. The trade's value depends heavily on appraisals the bill itself locks in, and the most consequential decision — whether a massive mine can operate there and under what conditions — would be made after the land has already left federal ownership. For opponents, the defining cost is irreversible: Oak Flat is a specific sacred site and campground that cannot be replaced by acreage elsewhere.

outcome.mechanism: After a single subcommittee hearing in November 2013, the bill sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee with no committee vote and no floor vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Sen. John McCain introduced the bill on February 14, 2013, with Sen. Jeff Flake, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S1][S3].
The committee's Subcommittee on Public Lands, Forests, and Mining held a hearing on November 20, 2013 [S5].
No further action was recorded — no committee markup, no floor vote, and no House action — before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, Oak Flat stayed in public hands and under the 1955-era withdrawal from mining, so the Apache tribes and others who use the site came out ahead, and Resolution Copper gained nothing from this bill.

for.name: Sen. John McCain
for.role: U.S. Senator from Arizona; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the land exchange bill and pressed for the transfer of Oak Flat to Resolution Copper.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Flake
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, which was introduced 'for himself and Mr. Flake.'

for.name: Resolution Copper Mining, LLC
for.role: Mining company seeking the land for a copper mine
for.what_they_did: Lobbied for legislation directing the federal land exchange, which was written around the company and names it as the recipient of the federal parcel.

against.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a committee vote; the record shows referral and one subcommittee hearing but no markup in nearly two years.

against.name: San Carlos Apache Tribe
against.role: Apache tribe for whom Oak Flat is sacred
against.what_they_did: Campaigned publicly against the transfer of Oak Flat to Resolution Copper.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so there was no roll call; its sponsorship was entirely Republican (McCain and Flake), while the committee chairman who declined to advance it was a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would hand the company full title to 2,422 acres of national forest land containing a major copper deposit, replacing conditional claim rights with ownership. Once private, the mine would operate under private-land rules, and the bill's payment to the government applies only to production above an appraisal-set baseline.

industries.industry: Public land recreation and conservation users
industries.note: Oak Flat includes a developed campground and recreation area that would be conveyed to a private company for mining, though the bill compensates with conservation parcels elsewhere and requires Apache Leap surface protection.
